DTECH-CTX-G1.title: Quarrystone take-home: Pager Quiet Windows (problem statement)
DTECH-CTX-G1.text:
QUARRYSTONE ANALYTICS - PLATFORM TEAM TAKE-HOME (v3)
Problem: Pager Quiet Windows

Background
Our on-call tool lets engineers schedule "quiet windows" during which non-critical pages for a host are held back. Engineers create windows independently, so the list for one host arrives unsorted and often overlapping. Before we push windows to the pager we collapse them into the smallest equivalent list.

Part 1: merge_windows(windows, grace)
Input:
- windows: a list of pairs [start, end], in integer minutes since the start of the quarter. A window covers minute start (inclusive) up to end (exclusive), so [10, 20] covers 10 minutes.
- grace: an integer number of minutes.

Rules:
1. If any window has end < start, raise ValueError with the message "inverted window at index i", where i is the index of the FIRST such window in the input list as given (before any sorting).
2. A window with end == start covers no time and is dropped silently. A dropped window must not bridge two other windows.
3. After sorting by start, a window merges into the current merged window when its start <= current end + grace. Windows that touch (next start == current end) therefore always merge, even with grace 0.
4. Grace only decides whether two windows merge; it never extends a window. A merged window ends at the largest end among the windows it absorbed.
5. Return the merged windows sorted by start, as a new list of [start, end] pairs. Do not mutate the input list or the pairs inside it.

Examples
Example 1: windows = [[10, 20], [15, 30], [40, 50]], grace = 0
Output: [[10, 30], [40, 50]]

Example 2: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 0
Output: [[5, 12], [13, 20]]
([5, 10] and [10, 12] touch, so they merge. The gap from 12 to 13 is 1 minute, which is larger than grace 0.)

Example 3: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[5, 20]]
(Note the result is [5, 20], not [5, 21]: grace never extends a window.)

Example 4: windows = [[30, 30], [1, 4], [2, 3]], grace = 5
Output: [[1, 4]]
([30, 30] is dropped; [2, 3] lies inside [1, 4].)

Example 5: windows = [[0, 10], [11, 11], [12, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[0, 10], [12, 20]]
([11, 11] is dropped before merging, so it cannot bridge the gap between 10 and 12.)

Example 6: windows = [[7, 3], [1, 2], [9, 4]], grace = 0
Raises ValueError("inverted window at index 0")

Example 7: windows = [], grace = 10
Output: []

Part 2: total_quiet_minutes(windows, grace)
Return the total number of minutes covered by the output of merge_windows. A gap that grace bridged is counted, because the merged window spans it. For Example 1 the answer is 30, for Example 3 it is 15, and for Example 7 it is 0.

Constraints
- 0 <= len(windows) <= 200,000
- 0 <= start, end <= 10^9
- 0 <= grace <= 60
- Your solution must run in O(n log n) time. Our reference solution runs in under 1 second in Python for n = 200,000.
- Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+. Standard library only.

What we look at
Correctness on our hidden cases (including every edge case above), readability, the tests you write yourself, and a short note (under 200 words) explaining your approach and its complexity. Please do not spend more than 3 hours.

Live follow-up
In the follow-up interview we will ask how your design changes if windows arrive one at a time from a stream and the pager needs to ask "is minute t quiet?" at any moment.

DTECH-CTX-G2.title: Lanternfish design notes and retrospective
DTECH-CTX-G2.text:
LANTERNFISH - DESIGN NOTES AND RETROSPECTIVE
Author: Dashiell Marrow, SRE I, Cindervale Systems. Written December 2025 for the SRE team wiki.

Problem
The checkout path (cart-api -> pricing -> payments-gateway) had a p99 of about 1,380 ms against an SLO target of 900 ms. Traces showed unexplained gaps before outbound calls that no span covered. We suspected DNS but had no per-pod data. CoreDNS exposes metrics per CoreDNS replica, only for the queries that reach it, and it sees a client's search-domain expansion as several unrelated queries rather than one slow lookup.

Design
Lanternfish is a Rust sidecar built on the tokio async runtime, using the hickory-proto crate to parse DNS messages. It is injected into pods on the checkout path.
- The pod uses dnsPolicy None with a dnsConfig whose first nameserver is 127.0.0.1. Lanternfish listens on 127.0.0.1:53 over UDP; only the sidecar container gets the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability.
- Each query is forwarded unchanged to the cluster DNS service IP. Lanternfish times the lookup from the moment the query arrives from the application to the moment the response is written back.
- It exports a Prometheus histogram, lanternfish_lookup_seconds, with 12 buckets from 1 ms to 2.5 s and the labels qtype, rcode and upstream. The queried name is deliberately NOT a label, to keep cardinality bounded.
- A counter, lanternfish_search_expansions_total, counts queries for names that end in one of the pod's search suffixes and come back NXDOMAIN.
- The existing Prometheus scrapes it every 15 seconds; no new storage was needed.
- The second nameserver line in dnsConfig points straight at the cluster DNS IP, with options timeout:1, so a crashed sidecar costs a one-second retry rather than an outage.

Why a sidecar
We considered three options:
1. CoreDNS metrics. Already existed, but aggregated per replica rather than per pod, and blind to how many expansions one application lookup triggered.
2. An eBPF probe on each node. Per-pod data without touching pods, but our GKE nodes ran Container-Optimized OS, nobody on the team had written eBPF before, and we estimated 4 to 6 weeks.
3. A sidecar. Per pod by construction, easy to remove, and about 2 weeks of work.
We chose the sidecar. The trade-off: it only sees pods it is injected into, and it adds one local hop to every lookup.

Rollout
Lanternfish ran on the 14 deployments of the checkout path for three weeks.

Findings
- 31% of p99 latency on the checkout path came from DNS resolution.
- The main cause was the default ndots:5. External names such as the payment processor's API have fewer than five dots, so the resolver tried every search domain first. On GKE that meant up to 10 failed queries (A and AAAA for each of 5 search domains) before the real lookup.
- A smaller share came from occasional 5-second stalls caused by a known conntrack race when A and AAAA queries go out in parallel over UDP.

Fix
- Priya Oduya (senior SRE) reviewed the design and ran the rollout of the fix; I wrote the sidecar, the dashboards and the analysis.
- Checkout-path pods moved to ndots:2, and the three external payment endpoints were changed to fully qualified names with a trailing dot.
- NodeLocal DNSCache was enabled on the cluster, which also removed the conntrack stalls.
- Checkout p99 fell from 1,380 ms to 910 ms, and DNS dropped to about 6% of p99.

Overhead and limitations
- Median added latency is about 0.3 ms per lookup; each sidecar uses about 6 MiB of memory and under 5 millicores of CPU.
- UDP only: queries that fall back to TCP after a truncated response are passed through and not measured.
- After the fix we removed the sidecar from 9 of the 14 deployments and kept it on 5 as a canary.
- It was never deployed to the other two clusters, and it has not been open-sourced.

items.question: Okay, let's go over your take-home. For example two and example three, walk me through what your merge returns and why the two outputs are different.
items.answer: I don't have the exact outputs for examples two and three in front of me, so let me walk through the merge logic and what drives the difference. The merge sorts the windows by start, then walks them, extending the current window's end whenever the next window's start is within grace of that end, and starting a new window otherwise. So the two outputs differ because of how grace bridges the gaps: where a gap is small enough to fall inside grace, the windows collapse into one and the bridged gap gets counted, and where it's larger, they stay separate. items.question: Let's warm up. Two sum: given 2, 7, 11, 15 and a target of 9, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to it. Approach and complexity, please.
items.answer:
For [2, 7, 11, 15] with target 9, the answer is indices **0 and 1**, since 2 + 7 = 9.

The approach is a hash map in one pass. For each number I check whether its complement, target minus the current value, is already in the map. If it is, I return the stored index and the current one. If not, I store the current value with its index and move on. That avoids the brute-force nested loop.

Time is **O(n)** since each element is visited once, and space is O(n) for the map.

items.question: We have an endpoint that lists shipment events newest first, and new events are being inserted constantly while people page through it. How would you design the pagination so nobody sees duplicates or skips anything?
items.answer:
Offset pagination breaks here, because new inserts shift every later page and you get duplicates and skips. I'd use **keyset pagination** on a stable, unique sort key. Since events are newest first, I'd order by created_at descending with the id as a tiebreaker, and the cursor carries the last seen created_at and id. The next page asks for rows where created_at is less than that, or equal with a smaller id, so each page picks up exactly where the last one stopped.

The catch is that new events arriving mid-pagination won't show up in the current pass, which is usually the right behavior for a feed like this. If someone needs a consistent snapshot, I'd add a snapshot boundary, either a max created_at captured at the start or a version column, so the whole walk stays on one view.

items.question: walk me through abba
conversation:
NATIVELY: The bug is that `enumerate` gives you `(index, char)` pairs, so `ch` is a tuple, not the character, and `right` is never defined. Trace `"abcabcbb"`: `ch` is `(0,'a')`, so `seen` keys are tuples and `right` raises `NameError`.

```python
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    seen = {}
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
            left = seen[ch] + 1
        seen[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

Unpacking gives the real character and index, and the `seen[ch] >= left` guard stops a stale index from moving `left` backwards.
items.answer:
ABBA is a synchronization pattern for a lock-free stack, and the name comes from the four states a pointer passes through: A, B, B again, then A again. The problem it solves is the ABA problem in compare-and-swap. Say a thread reads the top pointer as A, gets preempted, and another thread pops A, pops B, then pushes A back. The top pointer is A again, so the first thread's CAS succeeds even though the stack underneath it changed, and it can corrupt the structure or free a node that is still in use.

The usual fixes are a version or tag counter packed alongside the pointer so a CAS only succeeds if both match, hazard pointers that mark nodes as in-use before dereferencing, or epoch-based reclamation that defers freeing until no thread can still hold a reference. In practice I'd reach for a tagged pointer or a well-tested reclamation scheme rather than hand-rolling one.

items.question: Let's trace one. Lower bound binary search: lo is zero, hi is the length, while lo is less than hi, mid is lo plus hi over two, if a of mid is less than target then lo is mid plus one, otherwise hi is mid. Walk me through it on one, two, two, two, five with target two. Tell me lo, hi and mid at every step.
items.answer:
Array is [1, 2, 2, 2, 5], target 2, so lo starts at 0 and hi at 5.

Step 1: lo=0, hi=5, mid=2. a[2]=2, not less than 2, so hi=2.
Step 2: lo=0, hi=2, mid=1. a[1]=2, not less than 2, so hi=1.
Step 3: lo=0, hi=1, mid=0. a[0]=1, which is less than 2, so lo=1.
Now lo=1 and hi=1, so the loop ends and we return lo=1, the first index where 2 appears.

Can you pull up the two examples so I can point at the exact numbers?
INTERVIEWER (heard): And the complexity?

NATIVELY: Sorting dominates, so it's **O(n log n)** time, and the merge pass itself is linear since each window is visited once. Space is **O(n)** for the sorted output, or O(1) extra if I sort in place. That matches the constraint in the brief, which asks for O(n log n) and runs under a second at n = 200,000.
items.answer: The batch merge goes away. I'd keep an interval structure keyed by minute, like a sorted map or an interval tree, so each arriving window is an insert and a query for minute t is a point lookup that tells me whether t falls inside any merged window. That makes inserts and queries **O(log n)** instead of one O(n log n) pass, and I'd need to handle windows arriving out of order, since a new window can bridge two existing ones.

items.question: interviewer wants approach only: detect a cycle in a linked list and find the node where it starts. no code, 3 sentences max
items.answer: Use Floyd's tortoise and hare: move one pointer one step and the other two steps until they meet, which proves a cycle exists. Then reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the start of the cycle. It's O(n) time and O(1) space.

items.question: Implement an LRU cache with get and put, both in constant time. With capacity two: put one, put two, get one returns one, put three should evict two, and then get two returns minus one.
items.answer:
```python
class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.map = {}
        self.head = Node(0, 0)
        self.tail = Node(0, 0)
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return -1
        node = self.map[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._add(node)
        return node.val

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            self._remove(self.map[key])
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.map[key] = node
        self._add(node)
        if len(self.map) > self.cap:
            lru = self.head.next
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.map[lru.key]

    def _add(self, node):
        prev = self.tail.prev
        prev.next = node
        node.prev = prev
        node.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = node

    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev


class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, val):
        self.key = key
        self.val = val
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None
```

A hash map gives O(1) lookup, and a doubly linked list keeps recency order: `get` and `put` move the touched node to the tail, and eviction removes the node just after the head. The dummy head and tail avoid null checks at the boundaries. Time is O(1) per operation, space is O(capacity).

items.answer: First thing I'd change is the threshold itself. At Cindervale that took pages from about 260 a month down to 70. I'd know it worked by watching pages per week drop and the mute rate fall. What I'd leave alone is the paging path itself, since the signal is real, it's the routing that's noisy.

items.question: Why a heap?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Given an array of integers and a number k, return the k most frequent elements. For example one, one, one, two, two, three with k equal to two gives you one and two. How would you solve it?

NATIVELY: ## Approach
Count each element's frequency with a hash map, then keep the top k. The clean way is a bucket sort keyed by frequency: bucket index = how many times an element appears, so scanning buckets from the highest count down gives the k most frequent in linear time. That beats sorting the distinct elements, which costs O(n log n).

## Code
```python
from collections import Counter

def topKFrequent(nums, k):
    count = Counter(nums)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
    for num, freq in count.items():
        buckets[freq].append(num)

    result = []
    for freq in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):
        for num in buckets[freq]:
            result.append(num)
            if len(result) == k:
                return result
    return result
```

## Complexity
Time is O(n), one pass to count and one pass over the buckets. Space is O(n) for the count map and the buckets.
items.answer:
I didn't use a heap here, and that's deliberate. A heap is the natural choice when you want to avoid sorting all the distinct elements: you push each one into a min-heap of size k and pop when it overflows, which gives O(n log k) time and O(k) space. That's a good answer, and it's the one most people reach for.

I went with bucket sort because the frequencies are bounded by n, so I can index directly by count and get O(n) time. The tradeoff is space: the buckets cost O(n) instead of O(k). So the heap wins when k is small and memory is tight, and the buckets win when you want the linear bound and can afford the extra array.

items.question: heapify complexity?
items.answer: Building a heap from an array is **O(n)**, not O(n log n). Each sift-down is bounded by the height of the node, and summing those heights across all levels gives a linear total. Individual insertions are O(log n), so n of them would be O(n log n), but heapify does better by working bottom-up.

items.question: Have you run Postgres in production? Say there's a table with a couple billion event rows and vacuum takes hours. Would you partition it, how, and what gets harder once you do?
items.answer:
I've worked with Postgres, though not at that scale in production, so let me reason through it. Yes, I'd partition, almost certainly by time range on the event timestamp, since these are events and old partitions go cold. Monthly or weekly partitions, with the hot ones staying small so autovacuum has less to chew through.

What gets harder: you need partition pruning to actually kick in, so queries have to filter on the partition key. Unique constraints have to include it. Cross-partition queries and global indexes get awkward, and I have to automate partition creation and dropping, or you'll wake up to a missing partition.

items.question: Don't write code yet. Count the islands in a grid of ones and zeros, except the grid is huge, millions of rows, and you can only stream it one row at a time with memory for about two rows. How would you approach it?
items.answer:
The key constraint is that I can't hold the whole grid, so I can't do a normal flood fill. What I can do is track connectivity between adjacent rows as I stream.

I keep the previous row and the current row, and I label runs of ones in each row. Then I union labels that touch vertically or diagonally between the two rows. When a label's run ends and nothing in the next row connects to it, that component is finished, so I increment the island count and drop it.

The tricky part is that two runs I thought were separate can merge later through a lower row, so I can't count eagerly. I use a union-find over the active labels, and only finalize a component when it disappears from the current row. That keeps memory proportional to the number of active runs, not the grid size.

One thing I'd want to confirm: whether diagonal adjacency counts as connected, since that changes the union step.
